t: LeetCode 1678 — Goal Parser Interpretation: Decode With Two Characters of Lookahead
o:
The command string is a concatenation of the tokens "G", "()", and "(al)", which decode to "G", "o", and "al" respectively, preserving order. Example 1 decodes piece by piece: G()(al) becomes G + o + al = "Goal". Example 2 stacks five () tokens after a G for "Gooooal", and Example 3 mixes the order: (al)G(al)()()G becomes "alGalooG".

The grammar guarantees tokens are unambiguous, and the character immediately after "(" fully determines the token: ")" means "()", anything else means "(al)".

With length at most 100, any linear method is far faster than needed; the exercise is choosing the cleanest decoding strategy.
k: Only two characters of lookahead are ever needed: after "(" comes either ")" or "a".
Neither token contains the other as a substring, so chained global replacements are safe in any order.
A single left-to-right pass with an output buffer achieves O(n) with constant work per token.

a.i: Translate the two bracketed patterns with the replace-all primitive of your language. It mirrors the statement almost literally and is hard to get wrong because "()" never occurs inside "(al)", so the two rewrites do not interfere.
a.t: O(n) — each replacement pass scans the short string once
a.sp: O(n) — replacement materializes a new string

a.i: Walk the string with a manual index. A bare G copies through; upon "(" inspect exactly one more character to decide whether to emit "o" and skip 2 places, or emit "al" and skip 4. No pattern-matching machinery, one pass, constant extra work per token.
s: Scan with index i from 0 to length - 1.
If command[i] is G, append G and advance 1.
Else if command[i + 1] is ")", append "o" and advance 2.
Join and return the collected pieces.
a.t: O(n) — each input character is consumed exactly once
a.sp: O(n) — for the output buffer (O(1) auxiliary beyond it)

w:
Use the manual scan in an interview to demonstrate parsing skill, and mention the one-line replacement chain as the pragmatic production choice.
Pitfalls: advancing by the wrong amount after consuming "(al)", and testing for "()" after already matching part of "(al)". The input grammar guarantees validity, so no error handling is required.
Likely follow-up: decode a stream where tokens arrive in arbitrary chunks, which pushes you toward the scanner plus a small state machine.
